title: Juno and the Number Box
markdown:
Now, there was once a very curious little detective named Juno. Not just any detective. A number detective. Magnifying glass winking in the sun. Spectacles with a habit of tumbling down their nose. Juno loved to sniff out secrets in rows of numbers. Fingers danced, tracing sums in the air. Brow wrinkled — not with worry, but with the sheer delight of a good chase. And always, usually perched like the fluffiest, most chatty hat you ever did see, was Pipit. A robin, but not just any robin. A chirp that could make morning dew sparkle. Eyes that could spot a lost ladybug from the tallest oak. Always flitting. Always peeking. Always ready.

One bright dappled afternoon, golden sunbeams painting the mossy forest floor, they stumbled upon a peculiar box. Smooth dark wood, polished by time and perhaps a few gentle owl naps. A brass latch twisted like a sleepy vine. It would not budge. Etched on top, in letters that seemed to wiggle with mischief:

I have three friends. If one is 5 and another is 7, what number makes us all add up to 15?

“Ooh, a puzzle box!” Pipit puffed his tiny feathery chest, hopped on, and tapped the latch. Tap, tap, tap. Stubborn as a grumpy badger who had sat on the key.

Juno slipped on their thinking cap — a rather ordinary woolly hat that suddenly felt like the most important thing in the world. Spectacles slid. Juno shoved them up. They slid again, as if the numbers were tickling the nose.

“Let’s try some numbers, Pipit. If the missing friend was 1, then 5 plus 7 plus 1 makes 13. Not 15.” A wavy 13 in the soft earth with a twig.

Pipit fluffed. “What if it’s 2? Five plus seven plus two makes fourteen! Just one little hop away!” He hopped from foot to foot, which did not open the box, but did make a ladybug look impressed.

“Still not 15.”

This was one of Old Tom the owl’s prize creations. Old Tom was as wise as a hundred libraries, feathers like soft grey clouds, eyes like polished acorns. He adored leaving brain-ticklers, especially for Juno and Pipit. He knew Juno loved numbers. Pipit loved finding things. He also knew Juno would not be patronised by a box that opened for a lucky poke.

Three little nooks on the lid. One with a neat 5. One with a confident 7. The third empty, a question mark beside it. At the bottom, a narrow slot, just right for a number tile.

Juno’s nose almost touched the wood. “The riddle wants the missing friend. Five and seven are already at the party. What do we add so the three of them make fifteen?”

They drew in the earth: 5 + 7 = 12. Then 12 + ? = 15. “Three! Twelve and three is fifteen. The missing number is 3.”

Pipit chirped, a little confused. “We could try tapping three times! I have three hops in me!” He hopped three times. The latch stayed shut, like a sleepy frog with its mouth glued.

“That’s because the box wants the number, not the hopping.” Juno spotted a loose tile near a root. A 3, slightly sticky with pine sap. They wiped it on the woolly hat (the hat did not mind) and slid it into the slot.

Click! A tiny satisfying sound. The first compartment popped open. Inside, on soft velvet, a perfectly painted happy apple.

Pipit nearly fell off the box with delight. “We did it! First part!”

“Two more,” Juno said, heart thrumming. The next clue, beside the second nook: If one is 10 and another is 4, what number makes us all add up to 20?

Juno grinned, wide and confident. Same rule. Same hunt. “We need twenty. Ten and four make fourteen. Twenty minus fourteen is six. Six more!”

They rummaged. Pipit found the 6 under a leaf that looked, frankly, like it had been sitting on a secret. Into the next slot. Click! A plump juicy plum. Pipit attempted a victory roll, collided with Juno’s magnifying glass, and spent a dignified moment with his head in the woolly hat. Juno extracted him. The plum remained unpecked. Standards.

The last clue arrived as if the wood itself were showing off: If one is 9 and another is 2, what number makes us all add up to 18?

Juno was on a magnificent number-detecting roll. Spectacles tumbled, caught, shoved up. “Nine and two make eleven. Eighteen minus eleven is seven!”

The 7 tile was stuck to Pipit’s tail somehow. Pipit spun. The tile flew. Juno caught it like a very small, very important pancake. Into the final slot. Click! A bright cheerful red strawberry.

Old Tom’s hoot rolled down from a branch, warm as a hug. “Hoo hoo! Warmer than a summer’s day, and now quite hot enough.”

He had been there, of course, pretending to be a grey cloud. Juno did not need him to finish the sums. They had done the missing-friend trick three times: the number that belongs with the others to make the whole.

“Puzzle solvers,” Juno said, hugging Pipit, whose feathers smelled of plum-adjacent triumph. “Clever number detectives.”

Old Tom winked a slow knowing wink. The apple, the plum, and the strawberry sat in a row like a very small, very edible sum. Juno did not eat them. Detectives have standards. Pipit, who had lower standards and a faster beak, was gently discouraged.

They left the box open in the dappled light, three clicks still echoing, and wondered what other parties of numbers might be missing a friend — a pie, a fence, a flock. The woolly hat felt ordinary again, which meant the work was done. Spectacles stayed up, for once, as if even they had learned the rule.
characters: Juno (a number detective), Pipit (a robin), Tom (an owl)
